mappings.note: The stem has been overwritten with a chapter summary, but the stored answer shows the real prompt: do you keep a pet and how do you look after it. That is what a duty of care involves, LO-9.
List what you need to KNOW about a pet before you can look after it - finding out an animal's needs, which is LO-7, rather than illustrating care from the narrator's conduct (LO-9).

Work out what a Basra otter would need in London, using the climate notes supplied. Researching a species' needs before keeping it, LO-7; it stops short of judging whether an otter should be a pet at all (LO-8).
The trip to Basra and the five-day wait for mail are narrated; retrieval, LO-1.
Builds sentences with 'would' and 'used to', choosing by whether the verb names an action or a state. A grammatical convention, C-E1.3.
Classifies modifiers as noun, proper noun or adjective-plus-noun. Word-class and phrase structure, C-E1.3, not vocabulary.
Requires the learner to produce the incidents that show Mij's intelligence and need for affection - an answer built on textual evidence, LO-3.
Gathers what the text tells us about otters as a species. Information extraction, LO-1.
The naming of Lutrogale perspicillata maxwelli is narrated; retrieval, LO-1.
A fragment of a matching exercise that pairs Mij's actions with what they reveal about him; reading behaviour for what it shows is LO-2. The row's stem and answer have come apart.
Find Maxwell's own sentences and arrange them to support or refute given statements about his description. Evidence-based answering, LO-3.
The Londoners' astonishment is narrated; retrieval, LO-1.
The uproar on the aircraft is described in the text; retrieval, LO-1.

Builds noun phrases by attaching the right modifier to each noun. Phrase structure, C-E1.3, as against the lexical partitive exercise which is C-E1.1.
Matches partitives to their nouns (a pool of water, flakes of snow). Collocation and word meaning, C-E1.1.
'Pick out the words that tell you this' makes quoting from the text the marked skill, LO-3.
Duplicate of the species-naming item; narrated fact, LO-1.
Tick-the-answer check on Mij's first behaviour, which the text states. Retrieval, LO-1.

The second half - how Maxwell must have felt putting the injured animal back in the box - is an inference about the narrator, LO-2, which the text never states.

First asks what 'compulsive habits' means (C-E1.1), then retrieves the two examples Maxwell gives for schoolchildren and for Mij (LO-1).

Completes the text's simile 'as common as mosquitoes'. Recognising the comparison is a literary convention, C-E1.4, not plain fact retrieval.
MCQ version of the Mustellines item; a stated fact, LO-1.
Defective row: the stem asks how the otter spent his time while the options and key are years, so the item as scored tests when Maxwell travelled to Iraq. Either way a stated fact, LO-1.
The answer is the text's own image of 'a very small dragon'; the item tests recognition of that comparison, so C-E1.4 rather than the full description item, which is LO-1.
